analytic.title: A Feedback Scheduling Algorithm for Real Time Control Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper, the scheduling issue of periodic tasks with task dependencies is discussed. A feedback scheduler with frequency actuator and performance index is presented. Worst-case response time analysis that affects the real-time deadline miss ratio is analyzed. With the proposed scheduler, the schedulability of periodic tasks that have varied frequencies can be enhanced in the context of real-time control systems. Examples show that, this feedback scheduler can achieve high CPU utilization and guarantee a certain deadline miss ratio in real-time control systems without sacrificing the system stability.

Agent based scheduling algorithms and negotiation frameworks have been addressed in [21], [24]. Agent technology has been successfully used in distributed intelligent manufacturing systems and dynamic manufacturing scheduling problems. However, the negotiation and coordination between agents degrades the system efficiency and increases the cost. Other scheduling algorithms have also been developed recently [22], [11]. An integrated approach was investigated in [6]. This approach assigns task frequencies to control tasks in order to optimize a system performance index, consisting of control cost and tracking errors.

A feedback scheduler framework has been addressed in [8], [9] which can achieve performance guarantees in unpredictable environments and provide an adaptive scheduling algorithm in certain applications such as multimedia and internet servers. This approach can achieve a high CPU utilization and therefore is more cost-effective by allowing some tasks to miss their deadlines occasionally.

Unfortunately, scheduling hard real-time systems is far more complex than traditional real-time scheduling in the sense that (a) worst case execution times are typically more difficult to estimate because of task dependencies, and (b) certain aspects of control are usually difficult to integrate well with real-time scheduling. In hard real-time systems such as robotic or defense applications, a deadline miss is usually a disaster. For example, in agile manufacturing, a failure of an assembly job may not only result in a bad product, but also may damage the fixture [16].

Another issue is that all of the above scheduling algorithms assume that there is no task dependencies. They all assume that the tasks are independent and have no precedence constraints. Unfortunately, in some real-time applications, task precedence is unavoidable [14]. An example is robotic assembly applications. In this case, the scheduling algorithms are quite different. In [12], a task precedence graph is discussed that shows the required order of execution of a set of tasks, where each node represents a task or subtask and directed edges indicate the precedence relationships between tasks. A similar graph is presented and a matrix expression of the tasks is discussed in [14]. A possible deadlock situation is also considered in this paper. However, the performance of the scheduling algorithm is not mentioned and these scheduling algorithms are all open-loop, as they do not adjust the scheduled results on a feedback mechanism. Therefore, we plan to design and implement an integrated feedback scheduler that analyzes the worst-case-response-time so that it can meet both the performance guarantees and the task dependencies without missing deadlines.

This paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the scheduling problems related to this research. Section III discusses the proposed integrated task scheduler and the previous work that has been accomplished so far. An illustrative example is discussed in Section IV. Concluding remarks and future work are given in Section V.

div.head: II. PROBLEM STATEMENT
div.p: The problem we consider here is to find the execution order of n periodic tasks with task dependencies. The performance index represents the desirable features of the system such as the deadline miss ratio, the total CPU utilization, the total execution cycle time, and the total worst-case response time. For most hard real-time systems, the total deadline miss ratio is more desirable. To achieve this, a worst-caseresponse-time analysis must be provided. Note that the task interdependencies affect the worst-case response time and the total CPU utilization reflects the deadline miss ratio (for a dynamic system, if the total CPU utilization is below a certain limit, the deadline miss ratio can be always kept to zero, for example, for dynamic priority system, EDF can guarantee 100% CPU utilization without deadline miss and RM can guarantee no deadline miss for three periodic tasks under 78% CPU utilization). Here we choose the total worstcase response time as the performance index and the total CPU utilization as the controlled variable. To illustrate this problem, first the task constraints will be discussed.

div.head: A. Task Constraints
div.p: Two constraints that apply to all the scheduling problems are considered here: timing constraints and precedence constraints. Timing constraints usually refer to the deadline of the tasks. Precedence constraints are defined as follows:

• If task k must be done immediately before task p, task k is called the father of task p. • If task k must be done immediately after task p, task k is called the son of task p. • If task k has no relationship with task p, we say that task k is irrelevant to task p. • A task is triggered only if all its father tasks have been done. The goal of the scheduling algorithms can now be defined. Let us consider a hard real-time system with n tasks with the worst-case-response-time (WCRT) of each periodic task being R i . R i is associated with the frequency of the task itself and all its father tasks. Thus the following optimization problem can be formulated:
div.formula: min J = n i=1 R i (f ) subject to : n i=1 C i f i ≤ U, 0 < U ≤ 1 f i ∈ [f min , f max ] (1
div.p: where J is the desired performance index, U is the desired CPU utilization, C i is the estimated execution time of task i, f i is the frequency of task i, f is the frequency vector of all tasks. For each task, there is a frequency bound f i ∈ [f min , f max ] , which refers to the quality of service. If the frequency of any task is out of this bound, the task will then be declined and a deadline miss will be reported.

div.head: III. PROPOSED INTEGRATED FEEDBACK SCHEDULER
div.p: In this section, we will give the worst-case response time analysis and introduce an integrated feedback scheduler with frequency actuator. Previous work that has been accomplished in this regard will be presented.

div.head: A. Worst Case Response Time Analysis
div.p: Let us consider n tasks running concurrently in a preemptive multitasking system. The response time of task i is given by [2]:

div.formula: R i T j = R i T j + r ij , 0 ≤ r ij < 1(3)
div.p: Note that r ij is a function of Ri Tj ; the difference is due to round off to smallest integer greater than Ri Tj . Thus equation (2) can be rewritten
div.formula: R i (1 - j∈hp(i) C j T j ) = C i + B i + j∈hp(i) r ij C j (4)
div.p: Therefore, we have

div.head: B. Feedback Scheduler
div.p: From equations ( 1) and ( 10), we can define the optimization problem
div.formula: J = n i=1 R i (f ) = α1 D1 (C 1 + B 1 ) + n i=2 αi Di Ci+Bi+ i-1 j=1 rij Cj 1- i-1 j=1 Cj fj subject to : n i=1 C i f i ≤ U, 0 < U ≤ 1 f i ∈ [f min , f max ](11)
div.p: The goal of the scheduler design is to minimize the total worst case response time within the frequency bounds available for each task.

For a static multitasking system, all the parameters are known a priori. Since J is a function of the frequency f, we can use the Taylor series expansion to get an approximate value where ∇ J (f ) and H J (f ) are the gradient vector and Hessian matrix of J respectively. By solving equations ( 12) and ( 11), we can get the optimal scheduling results using linear programming technique [17]. However, most real-time multitasking systems are dynamic and some of the parameters may only be available on-line. For example, the dispatch time of each task is unknown and the execution time of each task could vary each time within a range due to network time delays. Therefore, we propose to use a feedback integrated scheduler to resolve the above problems.

div.head: C. Feedback Controller (FC)
div.p: From the task model that is addressed in Section II, at time instant kT , let us define the control related variables as follows:
• J(k): the real performance index at time interval k.
• C i (k): the estimated execution time of task i.

• D i (k): the deadline (also the period) of task i at time interval k. • R i (k): the estimated worst-case-response-time of task i at time interval k. • B i (k): the block time period of task i by its father tasks.
• α i (k): the weighting of task i.
div.formula: • U i (k): the CPU utilization of task i, U i (k) = c i (k)/D i (k)
div.p: The controller checks the real CPU utilization of accepted tasks and changes the frequencies of each task based on the weighting of the task. Here we choose a PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) controller as it does not require an exact model of the system. Adaptive control or Neural-Network based model will be considered in the future. The PID controller monitors the performance index (the total worst-case-response-time) and gives the control signal as follows:
div.formula: e(k + 1) = J(k + 1) -J(k) U (k + 1) = k p e(k + 1) + k i k i=1
div.p: e(i) + k d (e(k + 1)e(k)) (13) where U (k + 1) is the control signal, e(k + 1) is the error of the performance index, k p , k i and k d are tunable parameters of the PID controller. If U (k + 1) < 0 , it means that the CPU utilization needs to be increased; otherwise the total utilization should be decreased by calling the frequency actuator.

div.head: D. Frequency Actuator (FA)
div.p: The frequency actuator changes the frequency of each task based on the controlled variable so that both the stability of the system and the total utilization limit can be satisfied. From equations ( 11) and ( 13), we know that, the performance index J is a function of frequency f, task dependencies, execution times and task priorities. Let us define:
div.formula: min J(k) = h(f (k), C(k), d(k), p(k)) subject to : n i=1 C i f i ≤ U (k), 0 < U(k) ≤ 1 f i ∈ [f min , f max ](14)
div.p: where f, C, d, p represent the frequency, estimated computation time, task inter-dependencies and priorities. Note that the block time B i is related to the task dependencies. So we need to define the task dependencies of each task.

In our previous work, we have addressed a task-oriented scheduling algorithm (TOA) [14]. In this algorithm, each task is assigned a vector at the initialization time. Given a set of tasks Λ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , • • • τ n }, for each task, the expression is:
div.formula: τ i =< p i , d i , C i , u i , s i , f i > where p i , d i , C i , u i , s i
div.p: and f i represents the priority, task dependencies, estimated computation time, upper bound of the start time, start time and finish time respectively. Then we can use an offline scheduling algorithm to check if there is a deadlock situation. Deadlock situation only happens when two tasks are directly or indirectly the father task of each other. If there is no deadlock, we say that the task set is schedulable.

The frequency actuator adjusts the frequency of each task based on the total CPU utilization U (k + 1). Figure 2 gives the architecture of the frequency actuator. Note that the frequency actuator is a Single-Input-Multi-Output (SIMO) structure. The frequency actuator keeps tracking the performance index error and adjusts the frequency of each task based on the controlled variable. From equations ( 11), ( 14) and ( 13), we have

div.head: IV. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE
div.p: To test the proposed feedback scheduling method, let us consider an example. Table I gives a set of tasks to be scheduled. As we know, with the given task period, the total CPU utilization is 1.0576 which is generally not schedulable. Assume that the periods of the tasks are in the boundary as listed on Table II.

If all the tasks are adjusted to their upper bounds, the total utilization will be 0.8942. Therefore, this multitasking system is schedulable with our proposed feedback scheduler. Actually, with the proposed feedback scheduler, the optimum performance index with highest CPU utilization is 0.6750 under the given weighting parameters α i = [ 0.1 0.2 0.3 0.4 ].

From the given task period limits, we have the possible CPU utilization and respond performance index as Fig. 3. Fig. 4 gives the schedule process with the desired performance index. From Fig. 4, we know that, if the performance index is within the limits, (for instance, in this example, the limit is [0.58 0.71]), our scheduling algorithm can always achieve a good performance. Table III gives the calibrated task frequencies. From Table .III we know that, the worst-case response time will be: R i = [ 2 4 14 40 ]. Therefore, with the possible frequency bounds shown in Table III, we have the desired performance index h = 0.6750 and the desired periods of the task set: D i = [ 8 20 20 40 ]. As the worst-case response time of each task is less than its deadline, with the adjusted task periods, there will be no deadline miss.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we have considered the scheduling issue of periodic tasks by feedback control of task s frequencies. With the proposed method, the schedulability of periodic tasks that have varied frequencies can be enhanced in the context of real-time control systems.

For a given set of tasks with bounded time periods, a task set that is not schedulable may be made schedulable with the proposed feedback scheduling method. Furthermore, with the given method, the total CPU utilization can be optimized without a deadline miss.
Ongoing work will focus on the design and implementation of neural-network based feedback controller. Critical issues will also be considered, such as priority inversion and aperiodic tasks.
